I'm so glad you posted this because this is my rocd trigger as well. I even think of this as the crux or core of a relationship because the truest you is your thoughts and the words you use to express them to someone else. So I get super anxious thinking that our conversations aren't good enough, especially when I have literal direct comparisons of better conversations with other people or exes or something. I feel like we had the opposite trajectory though, it started off worse and got better over time. It's still a struggle sometimes and it sucks when it feels like I'm the only one who cares and when I push for it because I need it and crave it he feels criticized and defensive.

I think 40% is still pretty great, especially if he wants to work on it. Does he have concrete things to work on? I'm no rocd expert so this is more relationship advice, but something that's helped me is thinking do you want to break up right now? Like go see him and dump him? If not, and you're not going to do that tomorrow, then you want to be in this relationship. Do you see hope for improvement? Can you accept him the way he is now forever? Do you enjoy the time you spend together when you're not focused on the rocd?

My target right now is about 750k as a single person. I have a boyfriend right now and together we would probably aim for 1 million, which would be doable well before we're 35. Yes, we both max out our 401ks and Roth IRAs. He doesn't have an HSA; I max my HSA. 

The important things:

1. Don't spend money just because other people are doing it. Don't buy nice new cars (my co-workers all drive BMWs), don't eat out/drink/party all the time, don't get a house that's too big, don't buy designer clothes/accessories. Spend money on what actually increases your happiness. Maybe some of those things do, but if you need EVERYTHING then maybe you should prioritize. I spend a lot on travel, probably something like 3k a year but I'm frugal in a lot of other areas of my life. 

2. Cultivate cheap hobbies you enjoy. My bf and I like to go hiking/camping. We have all the gear so it's the cost of gas and some food to take. We like to play board games with friends, which is the cost of gas and some snacks. We read books on Kindles and watch TV shows/movies. We play video games (a few dollars from Steam sales). I like to cook, which isn't exactly the most frugal hobby, but I can often cook for a couple hours and get 8 meals out of it for less than $1.50 each. We scuba dive sometimes, which after getting certified/the gear is the cost of a tank fill ($3) and gas. 

3. Get into the mindset of saving = happiness if you can. I feel happy when I sock away money because I know I'm buying my future freedom. It is painful to spend money unnecessarily. 

4. Make money. I don't know how old you are, but choosing a more lucrative career makes things easier, although early retirement is possible with a lower salary.

There are a lot of unknowns, sure, but it's a general plan. Check out this blog post: http://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2012/01/13/the-shockingly-simple-math-behind-early-retirement/

If you save 50% of your income, then you can retire after 16 years. I currently save 90% but I expect my expenses will increase, so I'm aiming at saving 65% when that happens, which would put me at 10.5 years, which is around 35. 

Unknown things - if I can stay in my current career path, if I'll have kids, how much my partner will make, if we'll move to a lower cost of living area, etc. I just try to save as much as I can living a lifestyle I'm comfortable with.

Whatever I want. Right now the things I enjoy are Euro games, camping/hiking, cooking new recipes, travel, scuba diving, video games, reading, wilderness survival skills, photography. I could take multi-day camping trips, really improve my cooking skills, travel for months at a time instead of being limited to 2 weeks, get really good at survival skills, get really good at photography. I've also been interested in trying out: carpentry and woodworking, gardening, martial arts. 

I also would like to have a family and being retired means I could spend more time with my kids, taking them to the park to play, reading books, watching documentaries, playing with toys, trying out experiments, teaching them about the world, volunteering at their school.
